opus-5.5.text:
I think the engineering side is really underestimated. In agent-style RL, the rollout is no longer one prompt and one completion. A single trajectory might involve dozens of turns, tool calls, code execution, web environments, waiting on external feedback. So inference stops being a clean, batched, GPU-bound workload and becomes something much messier and much more like a distributed systems problem.

The first issue is the long tail. Some trajectories finish in a few seconds, others run for minutes because the agent keeps calling tools or the environment is slow. If your training loop waits for the whole batch synchronously, your GPUs sit idle most of the time. So you need asynchronous rollout, partial rollouts, some way to decouple generation from training. But once you do that, you introduce off-policy staleness, so you have to think about how stale the data can be before it hurts the learning signal. That's an algorithm and infrastructure co-design question, not something you can solve on one side alone.

The second is the environment itself. In traditional RL for reasoning, the reward is cheap: check the math answer, run a unit test. With agents, the environment is a sandbox, a browser, a codebase, sometimes thousands of them in parallel. Making those environments stable, reproducible, fast to reset, and isolated is a huge amount of work. Honestly, a lot of the gains I've seen come not from a clever loss function but from making the environment reliable enough that the reward signal isn't noisy.

Third is KV cache and context management. Multi-turn agents accumulate very long contexts. You want to reuse prefix cache across turns, but tool outputs get inserted in the middle, the context gets truncated or summarized, and memory pressure becomes the bottleneck. Inference efficiency for agents is really about memory efficiency and scheduling, not just raw FLOPs.

And finally, consistency between the inference engine and the training engine. If the numerics or the sampling logic differ even slightly, the log-probs you compute at training time don't match what was actually sampled, and in long-horizon RL those small mismatches compound and can destabilize training.

So my view is that for agentic RL, infrastructure is a first-class research problem. The teams that iterate fastest are the ones where researchers deeply understand the systems, and the systems people understand what the algorithm needs. That tight loop matters more than any single trick.

r001.rationale: The response discusses slow or variable trajectories and unreliable environments, but does not state that inference must tolerate execution failures partway through a run.

r002.rationale: It mentions numerical or sampling mismatches between engines, but does not attribute inconsistencies to heterogeneous machines or say those must be tolerated.

r003.rationale: It identifies GPU idling, environments, and memory pressure, but does not identify orchestration of resources such as CPUs and storage as a requirement.

r004.rationale: The response calls for algorithm and infrastructure co-design, but does not clearly state that training amid complex heterogeneous resources requires compromises between algorithms and engineering.

fable-5.1.text:
Fuli Luo: That's a good question, because I think a lot of people underestimate how different the engineering problem becomes once RL moves into an agentic setting.

When you're doing RL on a plain chat model, inference is relatively simple. You sample a response, you score it, you update. The rollout is one shot, and the main cost is just generating tokens. Once you're doing RL inside an agent framework, the rollout becomes a long trajectory. The model thinks, calls a tool, waits for the environment, reads the result, thinks again, and this can repeat dozens or even hundreds of times. So the inference system is no longer just a token generator. It's orchestrating an interaction loop with external systems, and the latency of those external systems becomes part of your training loop.

That changes a few things in practice. First, throughput. Trajectories are long and highly variable in length. One agent might finish a task in five steps, another might take sixty. If your inference engine batches naively, you end up with a lot of idle compute waiting for the longest trajectory. So you need asynchronous, fine-grained scheduling, where generation and environment execution are decoupled and can overlap across many trajectories at once.

Second, the environment itself. Tools, sandboxes, code execution, browsers. Each of these has to be isolated, reproducible, and cheap to spin up at scale, because during RL you're running thousands of them concurrently. A flaky environment doesn't just cost you time, it injects noise into the reward signal, and the model will learn from that noise. So environment infrastructure becomes a first-class part of the RL system rather than an afterthought.

Third, consistency between training and inference. With long multi-turn rollouts, small numerical differences between your inference engine and your training engine accumulate over many steps, and that can quietly break the on-policy assumption. You have to be very careful about KV cache handling, precision, and sampling behavior so that what the policy actually experienced during rollout matches what the trainer thinks it experienced.

And then there's the reward side. For agent tasks, verifying whether a trajectory succeeded often means running code, checking an end state, or calling another model as a judge. That verification is itself expensive inference. So the system ends up being three heavy workloads interleaved: policy generation, environment execution, and reward computation. Balancing those so that none of them starves the others is a real systems problem.

I'd say the overall shift is that RL for agents is much less about the algorithm and much more about the infrastructure. The algorithmic ideas are often simple. The hard part is building an inference and environment stack that can run millions of long, branching, tool-using trajectories reliably enough that the signal you get back is actually trustworthy.

r002.rationale: It mentions numerical differences between inference and training, but does not attribute inconsistencies to heterogeneous machines or say they must be tolerated.

r003.rationale: It identifies environment execution and reward computation as workloads, but does not identify coordinating resources such as CPUs or storage beyond GPUs.

r004.rationale: It contrasts infrastructure work with algorithmic ideas, but does not state that complex heterogeneous resources require compromises between algorithms and engineering.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that, in an agent framework, inference is part of a whole interaction loop. The model generates an action, waits for a tool or an environment, receives feedback, and then continues. So the engineering problem goes beyond making a single generation fast.

For RL, that becomes particularly challenging because you need many of these trajectories, and their lengths can vary a lot. Some finish quickly; others spend a long time waiting on tools or exploring. You need good scheduling and resource management so that those differences don’t leave your GPUs idle. At the same time, you need to track which policy generated each trajectory and make sure the training system interprets it correctly.

I would look at the entire loop: how quickly can we collect useful experience and turn it into a better policy? Raw tokens per second matters, but it’s only one part of that.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest shift is that inference is no longer just generating an answer. In an agent framework, the model interacts with an environment: it calls a tool, waits for a result, updates its context, and decides what to do next. For RL, you have to run that loop at scale to collect training experience.

That creates a different engineering problem from serving independent prompts. Trajectories have different lengths, tool calls have different latencies, and some environments fail or time out. If you wait for every trajectory to finish before moving forward, a few slow ones can leave a lot of compute idle. So scheduling, asynchronous execution, and managing the model’s context become very important.

But throughput alone isn’t enough. You also need to know which policy version produced each trajectory, preserve the information needed for training, and make sure the reward corresponds to what actually happened. If you make everything asynchronous, you then have to manage how stale the collected experience becomes.

So I would treat inference, the agent runtime, and training as one connected system. The useful metric is how efficiently that whole system produces experience that improves the policy.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says that some environments fail or time out during trajectories, identifying execution failures the system must handle.

r002.rationale: It mentions policy versions and stale experience, but says nothing about training–inference inconsistencies caused by heterogeneous machines.

r003.rationale: It discusses compute utilization and scheduling, but does not identify orchestration of CPUs, storage, or other non-GPU resources.

r004.rationale: It presents engineering challenges but does not state that complex heterogeneous resources require compromises between algorithms and engineering.
